newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists defy mass street protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists defy mass street protests.

text.p: Bulgaria's ex-communist Socialists defied 23 days of mass street protests and the threat of a general strike on Tuesday, announcing they would form a new cabinet under interior minister Nikolai Dobrev.
Sofia students staged their biggest rally to date, marching to the Socialist headquarters with soap and towels to mock the party's "clean hands" initiative to stop rampant corruption.
The three main trade unions called a general strike from Wednesday to protest against the deepening economic crisis and back opposition calls for immediate elections.

"We must fight them together -- the Union of Democratic Forces and the students in the streets, and the trade unions with their general strike," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told the daily opposition rally, which drew about 25,000 people.
The Socialists said they would invite all political forces to join them but were not optimistic about forming a coalition government and planned a cabinet of non-party technocrats.
Socialist leaders met their coalition allies and said they were willing to bring forward a general election to late this year, shortening their parliamentary term by more than a year.
"The Democratic Left expresses its will for early general elections and we propose that they should be held in the autumn of 1997," said a statement after the meeting.
The opposition has held daily rallies since January 6 to demand the removal of the Socialist government, which won elections in December 1994.

About 10,000 students, blowing whistles and rattling cans filled with worthless coins, marched to the Socialist headquarters behind a banner reading "I'm not a slave, what about you?" Police and journalists said it was the biggest student demonstration they had seen.
Trade union officials said the strike would start at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT). Evening rallies are faithfully attended, but one-hour warning strikes this month have had limited support.

"Let's go out in the streets and join the protesting children of Bulgaria, because they are protesting for a better future and against the bankrupt policy of one party." Dimitar Manolov, spokesman for the main opposition union Podkrepa, said.
Four army and police officers' associations appealed for calm, saying they opposed any use of force against unarmed civilians.
A police union spokesman said many police earned only 15,000 levs ($15) per month and were as badly off as the protesters.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov was obliged to ask the Socialists as the biggest party in parliament to form a cabinet, but on Monday he appealed to them to refuse the mandate and agree to opposition demands for early elections.
The opposition holds Dobrev responsible for clashes between demonstrators and police after protesters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.
He is seen as one of the party's strongmen because of the great access to information provided by his post. Police files from the communist era have never been made public in Bulgaria.
Dobrev has a week to name his cabinet, which must be voted on by parliament. The opposition says it will suspend its boycott of the legislature for the occasion.
"We'll be at the parliament to prevent the cabinet of Nikolai Dobrev being passed," UDF deputy leader Alexander Boshkov told Reuters.
The collapsing national currency fell below 1,000 levs to the dollar for the first time and banks called in technicians to reset their software to accept four-digit quotes.
Shops were empty but exchange bureaus reported a new flood of customers rushing to convert spare levs into dollars before hyperinflation eroded their value completely.
